sources.title: Largest bank heist in history: Binance hack rocks crypto industry | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Angela Barnes Published on 30 October 2026 - 6:05 GMT+1 • Updated 8:20 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Thursday it had fallen victim to a major hack that hit around $6.3 billion (€5.5bn) in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft. The company - the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes - posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses". ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Binance later said on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3bn (€5.5bn)". "We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~ $3bn (€2.6bn) frozen on-chain so far," it added. That would be more than four times the amount involved in what had been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5bn (€1.3bn) taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform. The Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor. Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said on Thursday it had "high confidence" that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing "robust on and off-chain intelligence". "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group - which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Fund freeze At about 0030 GMT (0230 CEST) on Friday, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement". "This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company said. The company's statement on X said an initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer", allowing the unauthorised party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions. "We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete. Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether - a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT - said his firm had frozen about $1.6bn (€1.4bn) "related to a potential Binance exchange hack". Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800m (€696m) in USDC. USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins", or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar. The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Crypto prices tumble For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform. The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, with the exception of stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins. At about 0400 GMT (0600 CEST), bitcoin and Ethereum were down 0.8%, recovering after plunges of nearly 5% and nearly 6%, respectively. BNB, Binance's native cryptocurrency, was up 2.7% after tumbling nearly 10%. The attack on Binance comes as many observers express concerns that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. sources.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, US immigration agents often work with their faces covered and do not wear identification. By Kali Hays Technology reporter Published 28 October 2026
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.
The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.
A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."
"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.
"We will update the public when more information is available."
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.
The information was put in a database named Icepick.
Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.
Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.
The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.
"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.
A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.
Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.
The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.
Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.
Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent , external , with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen

sources.title: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people | World news | The Guardian
sources.text: Skip to main content Skip to navigation The Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families. The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies. Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned. Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations. Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980. How the Hong Kong fire unfolded – visual guide Read more Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested. The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”. Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said. Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role. “I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”. But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added. Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served. She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing. Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster. Ashes and memories: one family’s return to the site of Hong Kong’s worst fire in decades Read more Since a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed. In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition. China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire. sources.title: Binance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist - France 24
sources.text: Binance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist - France 24 Skip to main content Advertising Binance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist Binance said on Thursday that a security breach had affected an estimated $6.3 billion in assets, potentially making it the biggest cryptocurrency heist on record. The world's largest crypto exchange said it had recovered or frozen about $3 billion, while the incident sent Bitcoin and other digital currencies lower. Issued on: 30/10/2026 - 04:48 Modified: 30/10/2026 - 07:47 4 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 (FILE) The logo of Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, which reported a crypto heist on October 29, 2026. © Justin Sullivan, AFP Binance , the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets . Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all hacking losses". An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko. Try again Cover image: PEOPLE & PROFIT © FRANCE 24 13:24 Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist , according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts. "It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report. "User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. "As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners."
